clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A client has a gravity-dependent external lumbar cerebrospinal-fluid drain with a prescribed drainage level. Which nursing action is safest?

options.A: Maintain the drain at the prescribed level, verify the setup after position changes, and adjust drainage only according to the ordered protocol.
options.B: Lower the drainage system whenever output decreases so that gravity produces a larger drainage gradient.
options.C: Allow unrestricted gravity drainage because system level does not affect the pressure gradient or overdrainage risk.
options.D: Remove the lumbar drain when a headache occurs rather than pausing and escalating evaluation of a possible complication.

semantic_correction.rationale: Contemporary external lumbar-drain protocols control CSF drainage through a defined pressure gradient or drainage target and require close clinical monitoring. A 2025 critical-care cohort describes a nurse-managed protocol in which the collection system height was set relative to an external landmark and adjusted according to intracranial-pressure and drainage targets; excessive drainage prompted raising the drainage level or stopping drainage. A 2026 multicenter trial protocol likewise treats suspected pressure-gradient-related overdrainage as a reason to promptly adjust or stop drainage under the treating protocol. These data support maintaining the prescribed setup and avoiding independent lowering of a gravity-dependent drain simply to increase output. No universal centimeter setting is appropriate across all conditions or institutions.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Maintain a gravity-dependent lumbar CSF drain at its prescribed level and avoid unauthorized changes that can alter the pressure gradient and increase overdrainage risk.

semantic_correction.source_locator: 2025 cohort — Lumbar CSF drainage: nurse protocol connected drain to sterile collection bag, set pressure gradient by system height, adjusted height according to ICP/drainage targets, stopped drainage for low ICP or neurologic change, monitored hourly to avoid overdrainage. 2026 DRAIN IVH protocol — drainage guided by clinical/radiological parameters; suspected pressure-gradient-related overdrainage or excessive output prompts adjustment of drainage settings by the treating protocol
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: External lumbar CSF drainage is controlled by prescribed pressure/drainage settings and close monitoring; drain settings are adjusted in response to defined targets or overdrainage concerns rather than arbitrarily lowered to increase output.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests preservation of prescribed drain settings and overdrainage prevention without converting a local research protocol into a universal numeric standard.

option_audit.A: Correct. It preserves the prescribed pressure/drainage setup and limits adjustments to the ordered protocol.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Lowering a gravity-dependent drain can alter the pressure gradient and increase drainage; it should not be done arbitrarily.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Contemporary protocols specifically use pressure/drainage settings and monitor for excessive drainage.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Headache can reflect low-pressure/overdrainage complications and requires assessment and protocol-based management, not independent drain removal.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone maintains the ordered drainage strategy while avoiding unsafe independent manipulation or removal.
cueing_check: All four options are drain-management actions of comparable length and specificity; no unique-length or absolute-word cue identifies A.
